title: Practice: symmetry in 3D
intro: Eight questions. Picture each shape being sliced by a flat sheet of glass: is one side a perfect mirror image of the other?

questions.prompt: How many planes of symmetry does a cuboid with edges 2 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm have?
hints: Look for a plane parallel to each pair of opposite faces.
questions.explanation: 3 — one cutting each of the three dimensions in half. There are no diagonal planes because the faces are not squares.

questions.prompt: How many planes of symmetry does a cube have?
hints: Start with the 3 planes parallel to the faces.
Then look for planes that slice diagonally through two opposite edges.
questions.explanation: 3 planes parallel to the faces, plus 6 diagonal planes (one for each pair of opposite edges), making 9.

questions.prompt: Complete the table for these prisms.
hints: A regular $n$-sided polygon has $n$ lines of symmetry.
questions.explanation: Each line of symmetry of the cross-section gives one plane along the prism, and there is always one extra plane halfway along parallel to the ends.

questions.prompt: Hannah writes four statements about prisms. Select **every** one that is **correct**.

options.text: A prism can have no planes of symmetry
A prism can have exactly two planes of symmetry
No prism can have exactly ten planes of symmetry
A prism with a semicircular cross-section has infinitely many planes of symmetry

hints: Every prism can be cut in half halfway along its length.
How many lines of symmetry does a semicircle have?
questions.explanation: a is wrong: every prism has the plane halfway along. b is right: an isosceles triangular prism has $1 + 1 = 2$. c is wrong: a regular nonagonal prism has $9 + 1 = 10$. d is wrong: a semicircle has only 1 line of symmetry, so the prism has 2 planes.

questions.prompt: How many planes of symmetry does a cylinder have?
hints: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
questions.explanation: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry (any diameter), so a cylinder has infinitely many planes through its axis, plus the one across the middle.

questions.prompt: A square-based prism that is **not** a cube (for example 2 cm × 2 cm × 7 cm) has 5 planes of symmetry.
hints: A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
questions.explanation: True. The square cross-section gives 4 planes along the length, and there is 1 across the middle: $4 + 1 = 5$. It only becomes 9 when the prism is a cube.

questions.text: A prism whose cross-section has $n$ lines of symmetry has [[a]] planes of symmetry. A regular 12-sided prism therefore has [[b]] planes.
hints: Count the planes along the prism, then add the one across it.
questions.explanation: $n + 1$: one plane for each line of symmetry, plus one across the middle. A regular dodecagon has 12 lines, so the prism has 13.

questions.prompt: Match each shape to its number of planes of symmetry.
hints: Planes = lines of symmetry of the cross-section + 1 — except for the cube.
